units.title: How fires begin
units.goal: Identify fire hazards without creating or approaching them.
text: Fire is a combustion process that can release heat and light. A hazard is something that could cause harm; risk also depends on the situation and exposure. Dry fuel near a heat source can create a fire risk.

Possible ignition sources include lightning, unsafe cooking, faulty electrical equipment and careless handling of flames. A learner should identify a concern from a safe place and report it, not investigate live wiring or test whether something will burn.
Fire can harm people, animals, buildings and habitats. A small-looking fire can grow quickly, and smoke can be dangerous even when flames are not close.

The activities here are virtual. Never light a fire for this lesson, burn rubbish, open electrical equipment or approach a real fire. Follow your school's emergency plan and trained adults' instructions.
units.challenge: Describe one fire hazard in a picture and a safe way to report it without touching it.

units.title: The fire triangle
units.goal: Explain the roles of heat, fuel and oxygen in a simple fire model.
text: The fire triangle is a simple model with three components: sufficient heat, fuel and oxygen. If a necessary component is removed, ordinary combustion cannot continue in the model.
Fuel is the material that burns. Heat can bring a fuel to conditions where it ignites. Oxygen, usually from the air, supports ordinary combustion. Oxygen is not itself the fuel in this model.
The model helps explain ideas such as cooling, separating fuel and limiting oxygen. These are scientific explanations, not directions for learners to fight a real fire.
Some fires involve additional chemical complexities. Trained responders choose approved methods for the actual fuel and hazards. A learner's role is to alert others and move to safety as directed.
units.challenge: Use the virtual selector to remove a triangle component. Explain the model's result without trying it in real life.

units.title: Classify by fuel
units.goal: Recognise common fuel groups and the limits of class-letter systems.
text: Fire classification helps responders recognise the burning material. Useful fuel groups include ordinary solid combustibles, flammable liquids, flammable gases, combustible metals and cooking oils or fats.

Paper and wood are ordinary solid combustibles; petrol is a flammable liquid; a fuel gas is a gas hazard. Some metals can burn under suitable conditions. Hot cooking oil is not treated as an ordinary paper fire.

Class letters vary across standards and countries. For example, the same letter can mean different things in different schemes. This lesson uses fuel names; a teacher should confirm the locally adopted class chart.

Energised electrical equipment adds an electrical hazard and requires suitable approved response. Do not assume one universal letter or one extinguishing material fits every incident. Learners should not operate equipment in a real incident.
units.challenge: Sort picture cards by fuel name, then explain why guessing a class letter without a standard can be misleading.

units.title: Control concepts, not experiments
units.goal: Explain why trained responders match methods to hazards.
text: Fire control aims to interrupt conditions that sustain combustion. Cooling addresses heat; separating fuel addresses fuel; some approved methods limit oxygen. These are conceptual categories rather than learner procedures.
Using the wrong substance can make a fire worse or expose someone to electric shock, splashes or harmful fumes. Never put water on a cooking-oil fire or energised electrical equipment.
An extinguisher's approved label describes its intended applications and limitations. Only appropriately trained people should decide whether it is safe to use equipment in an incident.

For learners, the priority is alerting others and following the evacuation plan. Do not delay escape to film, collect belongings, experiment with a fire blanket or operate a suspected faulty appliance.
units.challenge: Explain why a single 'put water on every fire' rule is unsafe, without proposing a real firefighting attempt.

units.title: Protect people & places
units.goal: Plan clear, inclusive safety communication and evacuation behaviour.
text: Uncontrolled fire can cause burns, smoke exposure, panic and damage to buildings and ecosystems. Emergency planning aims to protect people, including those who need assistance.

Learn your school's alarm, designated routes and assembly arrangements through official instruction. During an incident, follow trained adults and the site plan; do not use a virtual map as a real building's evacuation route.
At the assembly point, remain available for the school's checking process. Do not re-enter until authorised by responsible officials. Report someone missing to adults rather than going back yourself.

A useful safety poster uses clear words and recognisable symbols, provides the school's approved instructions and avoids frightening or blaming people. Never stage a real fire to demonstrate a poster.
units.challenge: Draft a safe poster that tells learners how to recognise an alarm, whom to follow and where school instructions can be found.

questions.prompt: Which can be an ignition source?
questions.answer: Faulty electrical equipment
questions.explanation: Electrical faults can generate dangerous heating or sparks.

questions.prompt: What is a fire hazard?
questions.answer: Something with the potential to cause fire-related harm
questions.explanation: A hazard is a potential source of harm.
options: Something with the potential to cause fire-related harm
A guarantee that a fire will occur

questions.prompt: What should a learner do about exposed damaged wiring?
questions.answer: Stay away and tell a responsible adult
questions.explanation: Live electrical equipment may cause shock and fire.
options: Stay away and tell a responsible adult

questions.prompt: Which is a natural possible ignition source?
questions.answer: Lightning
questions.explanation: Lightning can ignite suitable fuels.

questions.prompt: Why is smoke a serious concern?
questions.answer: It can contain harmful gases and particles
questions.explanation: Smoke can harm people away from visible flames.
options: It puts oxygen into every room
It can contain harmful gases and particles

questions.prompt: Which is suitable for this topic?
questions.answer: Virtual hazard spotting
questions.explanation: No real ignition is needed to learn the concepts.

questions.prompt: What is a safe response to an unknown burning smell?
questions.answer: Alert a responsible adult and follow the emergency plan
questions.explanation: Do not investigate a potential fire alone.
options: Alert a responsible adult and follow the emergency plan

questions.prompt: Which statement about a small fire is safest?
questions.answer: It can grow quickly
questions.explanation: Visible size is not a reliable measure of danger.
options: It is always safe for a child to tackle

questions.prompt: Name one possible fire ignition source.
questions.answer: For example, lightning or faulty electrical equipment.
questions.explanation: Identifying a source is not an instruction to create it.

questions.prompt: Name one material that could act as fuel.
questions.answer: For example, dry paper or wood.
questions.explanation: Keep real combustibles away from ignition sources.

questions.prompt: Why should learners not touch suspected faulty wiring?
questions.answer: It can cause electric shock, burns or fire.
questions.explanation: Report it to a responsible adult.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a hazard and a certainty?
questions.answer: A hazard can cause harm but does not mean harm is certain.
questions.explanation: Risk depends on circumstances too.

questions.prompt: Give one effect of uncontrolled fire on the environment.
questions.answer: For example, destruction of habitats or air pollution.
questions.explanation: Fires can affect more than buildings.

questions.prompt: Why is burning rubbish not a lesson activity?
questions.answer: It can cause fire spread, burns and harmful smoke.
questions.explanation: Use pictures or models instead.

questions.prompt: How should a learner report a hazard?
questions.answer: Tell a responsible adult from a safe place and follow the school's plan.
questions.explanation: Do not approach for a closer photograph.

questions.prompt: Why is a virtual model safer than a flame demonstration at home?
questions.answer: It avoids ignition, hot surfaces and smoke.
questions.explanation: Practical fire work is not for unsupervised learners.

questions.prompt: Does lack of a visible flame prove there is no danger?
questions.answer: No.
questions.explanation: Smoke, heat or electrical hazards may still be present.

questions.prompt: Name one group besides people that a fire can harm.
questions.answer: For example, animals or plants.
questions.explanation: Fire safety includes environmental responsibility.

questions.prompt: What should guide behaviour during a school alarm?
questions.answer: The school's emergency plan and trained adults.
questions.explanation: Do not invent a route or return for belongings.

questions.prompt: Why should fire safety information be easy to understand?
questions.answer: People need to recognise hazards and respond promptly.
questions.explanation: Clear signs and accessible communication help everyone.

questions.prompt: Which set forms the simple fire triangle?
questions.answer: Heat, fuel and oxygen
questions.explanation: The model needs all three components.

questions.prompt: What is fuel in the triangle?
questions.answer: The material that burns
questions.explanation: Fuels can be solids, liquids or gases.

questions.prompt: What is oxygen's role in ordinary combustion?
questions.answer: It supports the reaction
questions.explanation: Fuel and oxygen have different roles.

questions.prompt: In the model, removing a necessary component does what?
questions.answer: Stops continued combustion
questions.explanation: The model explains a condition for ordinary combustion.

questions.prompt: Which component does cooling mainly address?
questions.answer: Heat
questions.explanation: Cooling reduces the thermal conditions supporting fire.

questions.prompt: Which component is removed by separating unburned fuel from the model?
questions.answer: Fuel
questions.explanation: No fuel means the model lacks material to burn.

questions.prompt: Does the triangle authorise a child to tackle a fire?
questions.answer: No
questions.explanation: Understanding a model is not responder training.

questions.prompt: Which statement is accurate?
questions.answer: The triangle is a simplified explanation
questions.explanation: Real incidents need trained assessment.
options: The triangle is a simplified explanation
It replaces a school evacuation plan

questions.prompt: List the three fire-triangle components.
questions.answer: Heat, fuel and oxygen.
questions.explanation: All three have distinct roles.

questions.prompt: Explain heat's role in the model.
questions.answer: It supplies conditions needed for ignition and continued combustion.
questions.explanation: The exact conditions depend on the material.

questions.prompt: Explain fuel's role.
questions.answer: It supplies the material that burns.
questions.explanation: Fuel need not be a liquid.

questions.prompt: Explain oxygen's role.
questions.answer: It supports ordinary combustion.
questions.explanation: It is not the same as the fuel.

questions.prompt: What happens if the virtual heat component is removed?
questions.answer: The model no longer supports continued combustion.
questions.explanation: This is a conceptual demonstration only.

questions.prompt: What happens if the virtual fuel component is removed?
questions.answer: The model lacks material to keep burning.
questions.explanation: Do not remove real materials near flames.

questions.prompt: What happens if the virtual oxygen component is removed?
questions.answer: The simple model's combustion stops.
questions.explanation: Do not attempt to control real oxygen supplies.

questions.prompt: Why does the triangle not replace professional training?
questions.answer: It omits practical hazards and the details of real fires.
questions.explanation: Responder decisions require more than the model.

questions.prompt: Can oxygen and fuel be treated as the same component?
questions.answer: No.
questions.explanation: The model separates the reacting fuel from oxygen.

questions.prompt: Give one limitation of the triangle illustration.
questions.answer: It does not show all chemical and practical complexities.
questions.explanation: A model explains selected features.

questions.prompt: What should learners do instead of testing the model with a flame?
questions.answer: Use the animation and discuss the prediction.
questions.explanation: No real fire is needed.

questions.prompt: Who should select real fire-control equipment?
questions.answer: Appropriately trained adults or responders.
questions.explanation: Selection depends on the fuel and other hazards.

questions.prompt: Burning paper belongs to which fuel group?
questions.answer: Ordinary solid combustibles
questions.explanation: Paper is a combustible solid.

questions.prompt: Petrol is classified here as what kind of fuel?
questions.answer: Flammable liquid
questions.explanation: Its liquid fuel and vapour hazards require trained response.

questions.prompt: A burning fuel gas belongs to which group?
questions.answer: Flammable gases
questions.explanation: Classify the material, not just the appliance name.

questions.prompt: Why are cooking oils identified separately?
questions.answer: Their fire behaviour needs suitable specialised response
questions.explanation: A cooking-oil fire is not an ordinary paper fire.
options: Their fire behaviour needs suitable specialised response
They are the same as cold water

questions.prompt: Which statement about class letters is accurate?
questions.answer: They vary between classification standards
questions.explanation: Always identify the applicable standard.

questions.prompt: What extra hazard can energised equipment add?
questions.answer: Electric shock
questions.explanation: Electrical hazards affect safe responder choices.

questions.prompt: Which is the best first classification clue?
questions.answer: The burning material
questions.explanation: Fuel type helps identify the incident.

questions.prompt: Who should confirm the locally used class chart?
questions.answer: The teacher or appropriate local safety authority
questions.explanation: Different schemes use different labels.
options: The teacher or appropriate local safety authority

questions.prompt: Name two ordinary solid fuels.
questions.answer: For example, paper and wood.
questions.explanation: This is identification, not permission to burn them.

questions.prompt: Give one flammable-liquid example.
questions.answer: Petrol.
questions.explanation: Do not handle fuel for a classroom classification task.

questions.prompt: Give one flammable-gas example.
questions.answer: For example, a cooking fuel gas.
questions.explanation: Do not inspect or adjust a suspected leaking supply.

questions.prompt: Name the fuel group for a hot cooking-oil fire.
questions.answer: Cooking oils or fats.
questions.explanation: It requires suitable trained response.

questions.prompt: Can some metals burn?
questions.answer: Yes, under suitable conditions.
questions.explanation: Metal fires require specialist assessment.

questions.prompt: Why should a class letter always have a standard attached?
questions.answer: Letters are not universal across classification systems.
questions.explanation: Fuel names reduce ambiguity.

questions.prompt: Why is 'all electrical fires are the same fuel' an oversimplification?
questions.answer: Equipment can contain different burning materials as well as an electrical hazard.
questions.explanation: Fuel and energisation are distinct concerns.

questions.prompt: Why is an online class chart not automatically suitable locally?
questions.answer: It may use a different classification standard.
questions.explanation: Confirm the school or local authority's chart.

questions.prompt: What should a learner use to sort fuel examples safely?
questions.answer: Pictures or labelled virtual cards.
questions.explanation: Real fuels and ignition are unnecessary.

questions.prompt: Why should an extinguisher not be chosen from colour alone?
questions.answer: Approved labels and the actual hazards matter.
questions.explanation: Colour conventions and equipment differ.

questions.prompt: Does classifying a fuel make it safe to approach?
questions.answer: No.
questions.explanation: Classification is knowledge, not permission to act.

questions.prompt: What information should be included on a clear class poster?
questions.answer: Fuel names, the stated local standard and safe learner actions.
questions.explanation: Avoid unsupported universal letter claims.

questions.prompt: Which concept mainly reduces a fire's heat?
questions.answer: Cooling
questions.explanation: It addresses one triangle component.

questions.prompt: Is water suitable for every fire?
questions.answer: No
questions.explanation: Fuel and electrical hazards can make water dangerous.
options: Only if a child pours it
Only if the container is blue

questions.prompt: What should a learner do about a cooking-oil fire?
questions.answer: Move to safety, alert others and follow the emergency plan
questions.explanation: Learners should not tackle a real cooking-oil fire.
options: Move to safety, alert others and follow the emergency plan

questions.prompt: What should guide a trained person's equipment choice?
questions.answer: Approved labels and incident hazards
questions.explanation: Suitability and safety depend on the actual incident.

questions.prompt: Why is water dangerous on energised equipment?
questions.answer: It can expose people to electric shock
questions.explanation: Stay away and alert responsible adults.
options: It makes wiring safe to touch
It can expose people to electric shock

questions.prompt: Which learner action is appropriate during a fire alarm?
questions.answer: Follow the evacuation plan
questions.explanation: Escape should not be delayed.

questions.prompt: Does the virtual removal of oxygen demonstrate a home experiment?
questions.answer: No
questions.explanation: The control is symbolic and not a practical method.

questions.prompt: Why can a wrong response worsen danger?
questions.answer: It can spread burning material or add other hazards
questions.explanation: Fire control is not a trial-and-error activity.
options: It can spread burning material or add other hazards

questions.prompt: Name a control concept connected with heat.
questions.answer: Cooling.
questions.explanation: This names a principle, not an instruction to fight fire.

questions.prompt: Name a control concept connected with fuel.
questions.answer: Separating or removing a fuel supply by trained responders where safe.
questions.explanation: Learners must not approach or manipulate real fuel supplies.

questions.prompt: Name a control concept connected with oxygen.
questions.answer: Limiting oxygen using an approved method.
questions.explanation: Real methods need trained assessment.

questions.prompt: Why must water not be put on cooking-oil fires?
questions.answer: It can spread burning oil and cause severe injury.
questions.explanation: Move to safety and alert others instead.

questions.prompt: What should someone read on fire equipment before training use?
questions.answer: The approved labels, instructions and limitations.
questions.explanation: Training must be organised by competent adults.

questions.prompt: Why should a learner not move a burning pan?
questions.answer: It can cause burns, spills and fire spread.
questions.explanation: Do not approach to handle it.

questions.prompt: Why should filming not delay escape?
questions.answer: Conditions can worsen quickly while escape is delayed.
questions.explanation: Personal safety takes priority over recording.

questions.prompt: What should learners do if unsure about an extinguisher?
questions.answer: Do not use it in an incident; follow the evacuation plan and alert adults.
questions.explanation: Uncertainty is not a reason to experiment.

questions.prompt: Does understanding the triangle make all fires easy to control?
questions.answer: No.
questions.explanation: Real fires have changing and potentially hidden hazards.

questions.prompt: Why should real equipment be left to trained people?
questions.answer: Its use requires judging suitability, escape conditions and other hazards.
questions.explanation: A school animation is not practical certification.

questions.prompt: What is the learner's main priority in this topic?
questions.answer: Safe recognition, reporting and evacuation.
questions.explanation: The lesson is not firefighting training.

questions.prompt: Give one reason not to collect belongings during evacuation.
questions.answer: It delays leaving and can expose people to worsening danger.
questions.explanation: Follow the school's emergency plan.

questions.prompt: What should determine a real evacuation route?
questions.answer: The site's approved emergency plan
questions.explanation: Every site has its own layout and hazards.

questions.prompt: What should a learner do at the assembly point?
questions.answer: Follow the school's checking instructions
questions.explanation: Accounting for people helps the response.

questions.prompt: Who authorises re-entry after an incident?
questions.answer: Responsible officials following the emergency plan
questions.explanation: Visible calm does not prove a building is safe.
options: Responsible officials following the emergency plan

questions.prompt: What should you do if someone may be missing?
questions.answer: Tell a responsible adult
questions.explanation: Do not create another casualty by re-entering.

questions.prompt: Which makes a useful safety poster?
questions.answer: Clear approved instructions
questions.explanation: Accuracy and accessibility matter.

questions.prompt: Why should evacuation planning include people needing assistance?
questions.answer: Everyone needs an appropriate safe plan
questions.explanation: Inclusive planning reduces avoidable risk.
options: Everyone needs an appropriate safe plan

questions.prompt: What is the role of a school drill?
questions.answer: Practise the approved response safely
questions.explanation: A drill is organised practice, not a real ignition.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the virtual route is correct?
questions.answer: It teaches an idea, not your actual school route
questions.explanation: Use the real site's approved plan.
options: It teaches an idea, not your actual school route
It guarantees all exits are safe
It is a live emergency map

questions.prompt: Name two possible harms from fire.
questions.answer: For example, burns and smoke exposure.
questions.explanation: Property and ecosystems can also be harmed.

questions.prompt: Why is an assembly point useful?
questions.answer: It supports organised checking and coordination.
questions.explanation: Follow the school's designated arrangement.

questions.prompt: What should you do before returning to a building?
questions.answer: Wait for authorisation under the emergency plan.
questions.explanation: Do not decide from the absence of visible flames.

questions.prompt: How should a missing-person concern be shared?
questions.answer: Tell a responsible adult promptly and clearly.
questions.explanation: Do not re-enter to search.

questions.prompt: Give one way to make safety information accessible.
questions.answer: For example, clear language and suitable symbols, with support for different needs.
questions.explanation: Communication should be understandable to its audience.

questions.prompt: Why is blame unhelpful in a safety poster?
questions.answer: It can discourage reporting and distract from safe action.
questions.explanation: Use respectful, practical instructions.

questions.prompt: What should a poster use instead of a guessed emergency number?
questions.answer: The school or local authority's verified contact instructions.
questions.explanation: Emergency information must be accurate.

questions.prompt: Why should learners know the alarm before an incident?
questions.answer: It helps them recognise and follow the intended response.
questions.explanation: Training reduces confusion.

questions.prompt: Who should help plan assistance for a learner with access needs?
questions.answer: Responsible school staff with the learner and appropriate support.
questions.explanation: Do not leave assistance to improvisation during danger.

questions.prompt: What must never be staged to make a fire-safety video exciting?
questions.answer: A real fire or unsafe incident.
questions.explanation: Use drawings and virtual scenes.

questions.prompt: How can learners contribute to community safety?
questions.answer: Share accurate, approved safety information and report hazards safely.
questions.explanation: Do not conduct independent fire investigations.

questions.prompt: What is a respectful response when a peer is worried during a drill?
questions.answer: Follow staff guidance and offer calm support without blocking the plan.
questions.explanation: Safety practice should not become teasing.
